assets.domain: Growth vs. Fixed Mindset | Attribution Theory
assets.visual_frame_description: A glass-walled executive boardroom at dusk, with a long walnut table and seven executives seated around it. A stern CEO at the head gestures dismissively at a rejected product sketch while two engineers exchange nervous glances. Along the right edge of the screen sit three labeled columns: Fixed-mindset leader, Growth-mindset leader, and Groupthink dynamic.
assets.player_mission: Read each behavior card that slides onto the table and sort it into the column it best reflects. Sort all six behaviors, then confirm which column represents the leadership pattern a good-to-great leader would model.
key_concepts: Fixed-mindset leaders must repeatedly affirm their superiority and treat the company as a platform for proving it.
Growth-mindset leaders constantly try to improve, surround themselves with the most able people, and look squarely at their own mistakes.
Jim Collins's good-to-great leaders were self-effacing, asked questions, and could confront the most brutal answers while keeping faith they would succeed.
Alan Wurtzel of Circuit City held boardroom debates, pressing with 'Why, why, why?' until he understood the full picture.
Jack Welch went directly to front-line employees in factories like the Louisville refrigerator plant to find out what was really going on.
Lee Iacocca silenced critics, declaring the rounder cars looked like flying potatoes, and that ended the debate.
Irving Janis popularized groupthink: everyone in a group starts thinking alike and no one takes a critical stance.
Groupthink can arise when people put unlimited faith in a talented leader who is seen as a genius that never errs.
In Robert Wood's group study, growth-mindset groups stated honest opinions and disagreements while fixed-mindset groups fell into groupthink.
A company that cannot self-correct cannot thrive, and the fixed mindset blocks self-correction.
Rich Kinder, the only top Enron executive asking 'Are we smoking our own dope?', had his days numbered.
Morgan McCall noted people often like the things that work against their growth, avoiding criticism and new skills.
assets.theory_summary: This matrix tests the fixed-versus-growth leadership distinction: fixed-mindset leaders suppress dissent and defend superiority, while growth-mindset leaders invite questions, feedback, and self-correction. Dweck grounds this in Jim Collins's Good to Great findings and the Wood group study, where growth-mindset groups openly disagreed while fixed-mindset groups slipped into groupthink.

credibility.basis: Empirical education psychology (Dweck's mindset research; replication nuance)

assets.question: Sort each executive behavior into the column it reflects, then choose the column that a good-to-great leader would model.

rows.label: Rejects the new car design the team proposed, declaring the rounder cars 'look like flying potatoes' and closing the debate.
Runs boardroom debates, pressing with 'Why, why, why?' until the full picture emerges, as Alan Wurtzel did at Circuit City.
Advisors suspend their judgment because they believe the leader has the Midas touch and cannot lose.
Visits the factory floor and asks assembly-line workers directly what is going on, as Jack Welch did in Louisville.
Fires executives who question whether the company is fooling itself.
Assigns someone to play devil's advocate so the team can see the holes in its own plan.

distractors: Sorting Wurtzel's boardroom debates into the fixed column because a prosecutor is aggressive.
Sorting the devil's advocate row into the groupthink column because any assigned role signals conformity.
Sorting Welch's factory visits into the fixed column because he was a larger-than-life figure with an ego he held in check.
assets.explanation: The rows capture the chapter's contrast: fixed-mindset leaders suppress dissent and claim superiority (Iacocca's 'flying potatoes' and the firing of dissenting executives), while growth-mindset leaders like Wurtzel and Welch question, listen, and invite challenge to improve. Groupthink is the collective silence that results when faith in a genius leader or fear of disapproval suppresses independent judgment, which the Wood group study linked to fixed mindsets. The growth behaviors are the hallmark of Jim Collins's good-to-great leaders.

assets.domain: Growth vs. Fixed Mindset | Attribution Theory
assets.topic: Organizational Mindsets: Culture of Genius vs. Culture of Development
assets.visual_frame_description: A muted office lobby where a wall screen cycles through anonymized employee-survey responses from a study of large corporations. On the left is a column labeled Culture of genius, on the right Culture of development, and in the center Groupthink posture. A row of employee avatars watches the player sort each survey statement into its home column.
assets.player_mission: Sort each employee-survey statement into the organizational mindset it reveals, then identify which column Dweck's study shows produces trust, innovation, and ethical behavior.
key_concepts: An organization as a whole can hold a pervasive belief that talent is just fixed or that talent can be developed in all employees.
Dweck's team labeled fixed-mindset companies a 'culture of genius' and growth-mindset companies a 'culture of development.'
Employees in growth-mindset companies report far more trust in the company and a stronger sense of empowerment and ownership.
Employees in fixed-mindset companies express a greater interest in leaving for another company.
Employees in growth-mindset companies say their organization supports reasonable risk-taking, innovation, and creativity.
Employees in fixed-mindset companies report more cheating, taking shortcuts, cutting corners, and hiding information.
Supervisors in growth-mindset companies rate employees as more collaborative, committed to learning, innovative, and higher in management potential.
Dweck notes the irony that fixed-mindset companies hire and reward talent, then find themselves asking 'Where's the talent?' because it is not flourishing.
An organization's mindset shapes ethical behavior, not just performance.
Presenting skills as learnable and managers as resources for learning are elements of a growth-mindset environment.
assets.theory_summary: This matrix tests whether organizational mindset, a culture of genius versus a culture of development, shapes employee trust, commitment, innovation, and ethics. Dweck found that employees converge on a shared belief about talent that predicts risk-taking, ethical behavior, and whether talent flourishes.

credibility.basis: Empirical education psychology (Dweck's mindset research; replication nuance)

assets.question: Sort each employee-survey statement into the organizational mindset it reveals, then choose the column that Dweck's study shows produces trust, innovation, and ethical behavior.

rows.label: 'When it comes to being successful, this company seems to believe that people have a certain amount of talent and they can't really do much to change it.'
'This company genuinely values the personal development and growth of its employees.'
'In this company there is a lot of cheating, taking shortcuts, and cutting corners.'
'This company genuinely supports risk-taking and will support me even if I fail.'
'We got to the point where we thought we were bulletproof.'
'This company values natural intelligence and business talent more than any other characteristics.'
'People are encouraged to be innovative in this company; creativity is welcomed.'

distractors: Classifying the 'cheating, taking shortcuts' statement as growth because growth implies flexibility.
Treating 'we thought we were bulletproof' as a sign of healthy confidence rather than groupthink.
Placing 'values natural intelligence and business talent' in the development column because talent is a plus.
assets.explanation: Dweck asked diverse employee samples whether their company believed talent was fixed or developable and found strong within-company consensus forming a culture of genius or a culture of development. Employees in growth-mindset companies reported more trust, ownership, commitment, and support for risk-taking and innovation, while employees in fixed-mindset companies reported more cheating, secret-keeping, and a desire to leave. The 'we were bulletproof' row captures the Enron-style belief that follows when a group gets carried away with its brilliance.

assets.domain: Growth vs. Fixed Mindset | Attribution Theory
assets.topic: Groupthink and the Dissent That Prevents It
assets.visual_frame_description: A dim decision room modeled on the Bay of Pigs era: advisers seated in a semicircle around a confident leader while a ticker of historical episodes scrolls along the top. Three columns are open beneath: Groupthink symptom, Anti-groupthink mechanism, and Fixed-mindset suppression of dissent. A clock in the corner suggests a catastrophic decision is imminent.
assets.player_mission: Sort each decision-making episode into the dynamic it illustrates, then identify which dynamic Dweck warns can lead to catastrophic decisions.
key_concepts: Irving Janis popularized groupthink in the early 1970s: everyone in a group starts thinking alike and no one takes a critical stance.
Groupthink can lead to catastrophic decisions, as in the disastrous Bay of Pigs invasion.
Kennedy's advisers suspended their judgment because they had unbounded faith in his ability and luck.
Arthur Schlesinger noted that had one senior advisor opposed the adventure, Kennedy would likely have canceled it.
Churchill created a special department whose job was to give him all the worst news so he would not be groupthinked into false security.
Alfred P. Sloan, CEO of General Motors, proposed postponing a unanimous decision to give the group time to develop disagreement.
Herodotus reported that the ancient Persians reconsidered their sober decisions while intoxicated to prevent groupthink.
Groupthink can happen when a fixed-mindset leader punishes dissent; people may not stop thinking critically but they stop speaking up.
David Packard gave an engineer a medal for 'extraordinary contempt and defiance beyond the normal call of engineering duty.'
Robert Wood's study showed growth-mindset groups stated honest opinions and disagreements, leading to fuller discussion and better decisions.
assets.theory_summary: This matrix tests groupthink, the failure of a group to take a critical stance because of faith in a genius leader, collective brilliance, or fear of dissent. Dweck argues the fixed mindset breeds groupthink, while the growth mindset, by relieving people of fixed-ability burdens, leads to open discussion and enhanced decision making.

credibility.basis: Empirical education psychology (Dweck's mindset research; replication nuance)

assets.question: Sort each decision-making episode into the dynamic it illustrates, then identify which dynamic Dweck warns can lead to catastrophic decisions.

rows.label: Kennedy's advisers suspended their judgment because they believed he had the Midas touch (Bay of Pigs).
Churchill set up a special department whose job was to give him all the worst news.
Alfred P. Sloan proposed postponing a unanimous decision to 'develop disagreement.'
Iacocca insisted the rounder cars looked like flying potatoes and allowed no difference of opinion.
An outside consultant asked Enron executives where they were vulnerable; nobody answered and nobody even understood the question.
David Packard gave an engineer a medal for defying orders and persisting with his display monitor.

distractors: Calling Churchill's worst-news department a groupthink symptom because it sounds morbid.
Sorting Packard's medal into the fixed column because defiance broke the chain of command.
Reading the Bay of Pigs silence as sound loyalty rather than suspended judgment.
assets.explanation: Groupthink, popularized by Irving Janis, is everyone thinking alike with no critical stance, and the Wood study linked it to fixed mindsets. The Bay of Pigs and Enron's 'bulletproof' belief are classic symptoms, while Sloan's postponed consensus, Churchill's worst-news department, and Packard's medal for defiance are deliberate mechanisms to force dissent. Iacocca's punishing of critics shows fixed-mindset suppression, the third column.

assets.domain: Growth vs. Fixed Mindset | Attribution Theory
assets.topic: Talent Praise vs. Process Praise in the Workplace
assets.visual_frame_description: A bright open-plan office on a Monday morning, with a corkboard of award certificates labeled Employee of the Day and a sticky-note wall of thank-you messages. A manager's review screen shows three columns: Talent praise, Process praise, and Overpraise dependence. Speech bubbles drift from employee avatars as the player sorts each piece of feedback.
assets.player_mission: Sort each piece of workplace feedback into the kind of praise it represents, then choose the kind of praise Dweck's research shows builds hardiness and a growth mindset.
key_concepts: The children of the praise-for-intelligence era have entered the workforce needing a sticker for every move.
Some companies give quarterly or monthly bonuses and 'employee of the day' awards to lavish rewards on the overpraised generation.
Constant reassurance and an inability to take criticism are not a recipe for success in business, where persistence and correcting mistakes are essential.
Praising a brilliant performance or the smartest idea reinforces the fixed mindset.
The right kind of praise rewards initiative, seeing a difficult task through, struggling and learning something new, and being undaunted by setbacks.
With the right kinds of feedback, even adults can be motivated to choose challenging tasks and confront their mistakes.
Praise for acting on criticism builds hardiness rather than fragility.
Dweck suggests it could even be praise for not needing constant praise.
The wrong kinds of praise lead children down a path of entitlement, dependence, and fragility.
Businesses may need to help develop a more mature and growth-minded workforce if the leaders of the future are to emerge.
assets.theory_summary: This matrix tests the distinction between talent praise and process praise in the workplace. Dweck's research shows praising intelligence pushes people into the fixed mindset, making them dependent on reassurance and afraid of criticism, while praise for process and for acting on feedback builds the hardiness that business success requires.

credibility.basis: Empirical education psychology (Dweck's mindset research; replication nuance)

assets.question: Sort each piece of feedback into the kind of praise it represents, then choose the kind of praise Dweck's research shows builds hardiness and a growth mindset.

rows.label: 'You're the smartest person on this team.'
'You stuck with that difficult client through three setbacks and learned something new each time.'
An employee who cannot function without a sticker or reward for every move.
'Brilliant presentation. You're a natural.'
'I admire how you acted on that tough criticism and revised the rollout plan.'
'Employee of the day' awards introduced to keep constantly reassuring staff.
'I'm proud of how you took the initiative on the stalled account.'

distractors: Classifying 'you're a natural' as process praise because it is positive feedback.
Reading constant reassurance needs as a healthy sign of engagement.
Treating praise for acting on criticism as talent praise because it addresses the person directly.
assets.explanation: The chapter warns that praise for intelligence and talent, the praise that created the praised generation, pushes people toward the fixed mindset where they need constant reassurance and cannot take criticism. Process praise for initiative, persistence, learning, and acting on criticism motivates people to choose challenging tasks and confront mistakes. The 'sticker for every move' pattern is the corporate extension of overpraising that firms now pay consultants to reproduce.

assets.domain: Growth vs. Fixed Mindset | Attribution Theory
assets.visual_frame_description: A conference room with two negotiators across a table, a printed employment contract between them with eight highlighted issues from salary to benefits. Three columns hover beside the table: Fixed negotiation mindset, Growth negotiation mindset, and Integrative win-win outcome. A results ticker at the bottom tracks the negotiation's value for each side.
assets.player_mission: Sort each negotiation choice and outcome into the mindset it reflects, then identify which column best predicts negotiation success in Laura Kray and Michael Haselhuhn's studies.
key_concepts: Laura Kray and Michael Haselhuhn showed that mindsets have an important impact on negotiation success.
Participants taught a fixed mindset about negotiation skills chose tasks that showed off their skills without teaching anything new.
Almost half, 47 percent, of fixed-mindset participants chose the show-off task, while only 12 percent of growth-mindset participants did.
In live employment negotiations, growth-mindset negotiators did almost twice as well as those with a fixed mindset.
Growth-mindset negotiators persevered through the rough spots and stalemates to gain more favorable outcomes.
Growth-mindset negotiators were able to construct deals that addressed both parties' underlying interests.
Growth-mindset negotiators came up with more creative solutions that conferred benefits all around.
The more of a growth mindset an MBA student endorsed, the better he or she did on the negotiation task.
MBA students with a growth mindset on the first day earned higher final grades in the negotiation course.
A fixed mindset about negotiation holds that the kind of negotiator someone is cannot be changed very much.
assets.theory_summary: This matrix tests how implicit theories of ability shape negotiation behavior. Kray and Haselhuhn showed that a growth mindset about negotiation leads people to choose learning tasks, persevere through stalemates, and reach more favorable and more creative agreements that serve both sides.

credibility.basis: Empirical education psychology (Dweck's mindset research; replication nuance)

assets.question: Sort each negotiation choice and outcome into the mindset it reflects, then choose the column that best predicts negotiation success in Kray and Haselhuhn's studies.

rows.label: Choosing a task that shows off your negotiation skills but teaches you nothing new.
Choosing a task where you might make mistakes but would learn useful negotiation skills.
Persevering through stalemates to negotiate almost twice as favorable an employment deal.
Believing that 'good negotiators are born that way.'
Constructing a deal that addresses both parties' underlying interests after initial failure.
An MBA student who endorses a growth mindset on day one of a negotiation course earning a higher final grade.

distractors: Calling the show-off task choice growth because it showcases confidence.
Treating an integrative deal as fixed because both sides compromised.
Reading perseverance through stalemates as stubbornness rather than learning.
assets.explanation: Kray and Haselhuhn found that teaching a fixed mindset about negotiation, through an article titled 'Negotiation Ability, Like Plaster, Is Pretty Stable Over Time,' made 47 percent of participants choose the show-off task, versus only 12 percent after a growth mindset message. In live employment negotiations, growth-mindset negotiators did almost twice as well, persevered through stalemates, and in harder tasks constructed deals serving both parties' interests. Growth-endorsing MBA students also earned higher final grades.

assets.domain: Growth vs. Fixed Mindset | Attribution Theory
assets.topic: Giving Process Praise in a Performance Review
assets.visual_frame_description: A bright, minimalist meeting room in a Seattle software office; Lena sits across from Marcus at a small table, her laptop closed and a spiral notebook between them. Marcus slouches slightly, running a finger along the edge of his notepad, while a window behind them shows the city skyline. The player sits in Lena's seat and must deliver the review.
assets.player_mission: As Lena, deliver feedback to Marcus about his salvaged rebranding campaign. Choose the response that rewards his learning process and prepares him for harder work, rather than praise that reinforces talent labels.
assets.scenario_setup: Lena, a 34-year-old product manager, is giving a quarterly performance review to Marcus, a 28-year-old marketing associate. Marcus just salvaged a rebranding campaign that failed twice in front of clients before he finally turned it around. Marcus has been praised his whole life as the smart one, and Lena can see he is anxious about being judged. Her goal is to keep him taking hard assignments and taking criticism well.
dialogue: Lena: Before we start, Marcus, I want you to know this review is about what happened this quarter, not about who you are.
Marcus: Thanks. Honestly, I'm still a little raw about the two failed pitches. I feel like I let the team down.
Lena: Let's talk about them. What did you do after the first pitch failed?
Marcus: I went back to the clients' notes, redid the messaging, and asked Priya to role-play the objections with me.
Lena: And after the second failure, when leadership wanted to pull the campaign?
Marcus: I pushed to keep it alive for one more round and revised the whole rollout plan based on what we'd learned.
Lena: That is exactly the behavior I want to reward. You struggled, you learned something new each time, and you acted on the criticism. That tells me more than any smart-sounding first draft.
Marcus: So the two failures are not going to count against me?
Lena: They count, as evidence that you know how to get up and adjust. I'm putting you on the flagship account next quarter.
choices: You're clearly the most talented marketer on this team. You pulled that off on raw ability.
You're so smart, Marcus. You always figure it out eventually.
I want to reward how you handled the setbacks. You sought feedback, revised your strategy, and kept going, so I'm giving you the flagship account.
Good job. But don't let it happen again. We can't afford two more failed pitches.
assets.theoretical_principle: Process praise (praising effort, strategies, learning, and response to criticism) versus talent praise
assets.psychological_breakdown: Option 2 is optimal because it praises the process: initiative, learning from failure, and acting on criticism, which Dweck's research shows builds a growth mindset and hardiness for future challenges. Options 0 and 1 are talent praise, which feels great but pushes Marcus into the fixed mindset, making him dependent on reassurance and afraid of future failure. Option 3 withholds credit for the learning and reinforces fear of judgment, the opposite of the growth-promoting feedback the chapter recommends.
key_concepts: Praising intelligence and talent pushes people toward the fixed mindset.
Process praise, for initiative, persistence, and learning, builds a growth mindset.
Praise for acting on criticism helps employees confront their mistakes.
With the right kinds of feedback, even adults can be motivated to choose challenging tasks.
Employees who were overpraised as children often need constant reassurance and cannot take criticism.
A growth-promoting workplace rewards struggle and learning rather than ready-made genius.
Businesses may need to play a role in developing a more mature and growth-minded workforce.
Growth-minded managers act as guides, not judges.
Feedback that promotes learning and future success is a hallmark of a growth-mindset environment.
The praised generation's need for stickers on every move is not a recipe for business success.
assets.theory_summary: This dialogue tests process praise versus talent praise in a performance review. Dweck's research shows that praising the process, the struggle, strategies, and acting on criticism, motivates adults to take on challenges and confront mistakes, while talent praise breeds dependence and fear of judgment.

credibility.basis: Empirical education psychology (Dweck's mindset research; replication nuance)

assets.domain: Growth vs. Fixed Mindset | Attribution Theory
assets.topic: Coaching a Struggling Performer: Fixed vs. Growth Managers
assets.visual_frame_description: A regional sales office with a whiteboard of quarterly quotas; Tom, 51, a sales director, leans against his desk while a younger account executive, Ravi, 29, sits across from him clutching a printout of his call notes. A window shows a freight yard below. The player is Tom and must decide how to treat a struggling performer.
assets.player_mission: As Tom, decide how to handle Ravi after three straight quarters below quota. Choose the response of a manager who believes people can develop, rather than a manager who has already judged Ravi unchangeable.
assets.scenario_setup: Tom's own manager, Priya, has suggested managing Ravi out after Ravi missed quota for three straight quarters. Tom read the chapter's research on managers who believe people can change and wonders whether coaching could turn Ravi around. His goal is to decide whether a struggling performer deserves development or dismissal.
dialogue: Tom: Priya keeps telling me Ravi is not a salesperson and I should let him go.
Ravi (from memory): I know I keep missing quota, Tom. I feel like I'm just not cut out for this.
Tom: Let's look at your call notes from last month.
Ravi: I mostly talked about our features and pricing. When clients pushed back, I just dropped the price.
Tom: What would you do differently if the clients pushed back on value instead of price?
Ravi: I'm not sure. I've never really been trained on it.
Tom: That's the thing, you haven't. Let's set up role-play sessions with our top closer, and I'll observe your next five pitches and give you specific feedback.
Ravi: You're not going to fire me?
Tom: Not yet. Talent is just the starting point. I want to see what you do with training and feedback.
Ravi: I'll put in the work. Thank you.
choices: Ravi, you're not a natural salesperson. Let's be realistic about your future here.
I've already made up my mind about you from the first quarter. Let's talk severance.
Talent is just the starting point. I'll coach you, give you feedback, and we'll track whether you improve.
This is your last chance. Hit quota next quarter or you're out, with no handholding.
assets.theoretical_principle: Implicit theory of ability applied to management: managers who believe people can change give developmental coaching
assets.psychological_breakdown: Option 2 reflects the growth-mindset manager in the Heslin, VandeWalle, and Latham studies: more developmental coaching, noticing improvement, and welcoming feedback. Options 0 and 1 are fixed-mindset stances, judging employees as competent or incompetent at the start and staying stuck in that initial impression. Option 3 demands results without offering a pathway to develop, treating improvement as a matter of pure will.
key_concepts: Studies by Peter Heslin, Don VandeWalle, and Gary Latham show many managers do not believe in personal change.
Fixed-mindset managers judge employees as competent or incompetent at the start and remain stuck in that initial impression.
Fixed-mindset managers do relatively little developmental coaching.
Growth-mindset managers give a great deal more developmental coaching and notice improvement in employee performance.
Growth-mindset managers welcome critiques from their employees.
Fixed-mindset managers are less likely to seek or accept critical feedback from employees.
Growth-mindset managers see talent as nice to have but only the starting point.
A brief workshop based on well-established psychological principles can teach managers a growth mindset.
After the workshop, managers more readily detected improvement, were more willing to coach poor performers, and gave more and better coaching suggestions.
Training and experience can often draw out and develop the qualities required for successful performance.
assets.theory_summary: This dialogue tests whether a manager treats ability as fixed or developable. Heslin, VandeWalle, and Latham found that managers with a growth mindset coach more, notice improvement, and welcome feedback, and that these beliefs can be taught in a short workshop.

credibility.basis: Empirical education psychology (Dweck's mindset research; replication nuance)

assets.domain: Growth vs. Fixed Mindset | Attribution Theory
assets.visual_frame_description: A Silicon Valley hardware lab with a prototype monitor glowing on a workbench; Nina, 30, a display engineer, stands between her manager Greg and the prototype while a calendar reads 'Vacation.' In a corner, a framed black-and-white photo shows David Packard pinning a medal on an engineer. The player must decide how Nina responds to an order to shelve her project.
assets.player_mission: As Nina, decide what to do when your manager orders you to abandon a promising display monitor. Choose the path that mirrors the Hewlett-Packard engineer who earned Packard's medal for defiance.
assets.scenario_setup: Nina's manager, Greg, ordered the team to shelve a promising monitor project to focus on a cheaper product line. Nina believes the monitor has real demand, but she has seen colleagues who disagreed get sidelined. The chapter's story of David Packard's medal for defiance frames her dilemma: follow orders quietly or gather real customer evidence.
dialogue: Greg: Nina, I'm killing the monitor project effective immediately. It's a distraction.
Nina: Greg, the customer feedback on the prototype is strong. We already have letters of intent.
Greg: I've decided. The board wants cost down this quarter, and the monitor is a cost sink.
Nina: (to herself) If I drop this, it dies. If I go on vacation and show it to customers, I might get fired, or I might prove the demand.
Greg: Do you understand? I need to hear you say you're done with it.
Nina: I understand you've made a decision. I'll take some time off to think about next steps.
Customer (later, at a trade visit): This monitor solves our exact problem. We'd order two hundred units if you'd build it.
Nina: (returning) Greg, I have purchase interest. Two hundred units from three customers who saw the prototype.
Greg: You went behind my back?!
Nina: I went in front of our customers. The demand is real. Can we reconsider?
choices: Greg, I respect your authority. I'll shut the project down and reallocate the team.
I'll quietly keep working on it at home and present it to you again in six months.
I showed the monitor to potential customers, got real purchase interest, and I'm asking you to reconsider. I'll take responsibility for the risk.
Fine, you're the boss. But I'm documenting that this decision is wrong so history judges you.
assets.theoretical_principle: The value of open dissent against groupthink, illustrated by Packard's medal for 'extraordinary contempt and defiance beyond the normal call of engineering duty'
assets.psychological_breakdown: Option 2 mirrors the Hewlett-Packard engineer who defied the order, gathered real evidence, and brought the company more than seventeen thousand monitor sales and thirty-five million dollars in revenue. Option 0 surrenders to the groupthink pattern in which people stop speaking up even when they think critically. Option 1 hides the disagreement rather than forcing it into the open, and Option 3 turns the conflict into revenge, which serves the ego rather than the company.
key_concepts: Groupthink can happen when a fixed-mindset leader punishes dissent.
People may not stop thinking critically, but they stop speaking up when dissent is punished.
David Packard gave an engineer a medal 'for extraordinary contempt and defiance beyond the normal call of engineering duty.'
The HP engineer, told to give up a display monitor, went on vacation and showed the prototype to potential customers.
The customers loved the monitor, and the company sold more than seventeen thousand units for thirty-five million dollars in revenue.
Hewlett-Packard's co-founder rewarded the engineer rather than punishing the defiance.
Leaders are sometimes seen as gods who never err, which suppresses dissent.
Workers seeking validation from leaders may fall into line behind them.
A growth mindset leads to a full and open discussion of information and enhanced decision making.
People can be independent thinkers and team players at the same time.
assets.theory_summary: This dialogue tests the value of dissent against a groupthink-producing leader. Dweck uses Packard's medal for defiance to show that open disagreement, even at personal risk, produces better results than the silence that fixed-mindset leadership enforces.

credibility.basis: Empirical education psychology (Dweck's mindset research; replication nuance)

assets.domain: Growth vs. Fixed Mindset | Attribution Theory
assets.visual_frame_description: A modern HR office at a consumer electronics firm; Dana, 33, a senior product designer, sits across from Alex, a recruiter, with a printed offer letter between them and eight checkboxes from salary to benefits listed on a screen. Alex's arms are crossed after declaring the salary band firm. The player is Dana deciding how to respond to a stalemate.
assets.player_mission: As Dana, respond to the recruiter who says the salary band is firm. Choose the strategy of a growth-mindset negotiator who persists through the stalemate and searches the full set of issues for a deal that serves both sides.
assets.scenario_setup: Dana is negotiating her job offer with Alex, a recruiter at a large consumer electronics firm. The offer is good but below market, and Dana must negotiate on eight issues including salary, vacation, and benefits. Dana read about mindsets and negotiation and believes her skills can grow with practice, but she has already hit a stalemate on salary.
dialogue: Alex: I appreciate you pushing back, Dana, but our salary band for this role is firm. Take it or leave it.
Dana: I hear that the number is firm, so help me understand the band. Is there flexibility in the role level or in the timing of performance reviews?
Alex: The level is set, but review timing could move up if that helps bridge the gap.
Dana: What about vacation and the signing bonus? I noticed your benefits package is light on parental leave.
Alex: The signing bonus has some room. Parental leave is standard across the company.
Dana: Then let's trade. I'll accept the salary band if the signing bonus covers the difference and the review moves to six months.
Alex: If I can get that approved, do we have a deal?
Dana: If we also confirm the vacation weeks in writing, yes. I want a deal that works for both of us, and I plan to be here for the long run.
Alex: Let me get the approvals. I think we can make this work.
choices: Fine. I'll take the original offer. I don't want to be difficult on my first day.
I'm walking. A recruiter who won't move on salary is wasting my time.
I'll hold firm on salary only. If you can't match my number, this deal is dead.
Let's explore the full set of issues. If salary is fixed, we can find value in the bonus, review timing, and benefits, and build a deal that serves both sides.
assets.theoretical_principle: Growth mindset in negotiation: persevering through stalemates and constructing integrative deals that address both parties' underlying interests
assets.psychological_breakdown: Option 3 reflects the growth-mindset negotiator in Kray and Haselhuhn's studies: persist through the rough spots and seek creative solutions that benefit both parties rather than fixating on a single issue. Option 0 surrenders value, option 1 abandons the deal at the first obstacle, and option 2 collapses the negotiation onto one dimension, risking a deadlock instead of an integrated agreement.
key_concepts: Kray and Haselhuhn taught participants either a fixed or a growth mindset about negotiation skills.
In live employment negotiations, growth-mindset negotiators did almost twice as well as fixed-mindset negotiators.
Growth-mindset negotiators persevered through the rough spots and stalemates.
In harder tasks, growth-mindset negotiators constructed deals that addressed both parties' underlying interests.
Growth-mindset negotiators came up with more creative solutions that conferred benefits all around.
MBA students who endorsed growth-mindset statements did better on the negotiation task.
Growth-mindset MBA students earned higher final grades in the negotiation course.
Negotiation skills can be cultivated and developed over a lifetime.
47 percent of fixed-mindset participants chose a show-off task, while only 12 percent of growth-mindset participants did.
A growth mindset in negotiation does not just mean getting one's own way; it also serves the other party's interests.
assets.theory_summary: This dialogue tests the growth mindset applied to negotiation. Kray and Haselhuhn showed that negotiators who believe the skill is developable persist through stalemates, win more favorable outcomes, and construct integrative deals that serve both sides.

credibility.basis: Empirical education psychology (Dweck's mindset research; replication nuance)

assets.domain: Growth vs. Fixed Mindset | Attribution Theory
assets.topic: Welcoming Bad News: CEO Disease vs. Honest Feedback
assets.visual_frame_description: A corner office at an energy company on the evening of a board review; Viktor, 58, the founder-CEO, stands by a window with the skyline behind him while his COO Maria holds a spreadsheet marked Revised Forecast Downward. A portrait of the CEO hangs on the wall, and a small plaque reads 'Are we smoking our own dope?' The player is Viktor facing genuinely bad news.
assets.player_mission: As Viktor, respond when your COO brings you genuinely bad news about missing earnings targets. Choose the response of a leader who welcomes the worst news rather than the one who silences critics.
assets.scenario_setup: Viktor has spent months surrounded by executives who confirm his brilliance, and his company is about to miss its earnings targets. His COO, Maria, is the only one who keeps asking hard questions. The scene parallels Rich Kinder at Enron asking whether the firm was fooling itself, and Churchill's special department that delivered only the worst news.
dialogue: Maria: Viktor, I have to be direct. We are going to miss Q2 targets, and our pipeline math has been overstated.
Viktor: (coldly) That can't be right. My people told me we were ahead.
Maria: That's exactly why I'm here. Your people are telling you what you want to hear. I'm telling you what the numbers show.
Viktor: Are you sure you're not covering for your own mistakes?
Maria: I'm not covering anything up. I'm the only one in this room who asked if we were fooling ourselves, and the answer is yes.
Viktor: (pause) Tell me the worst part first. I'd rather hear the worst news now than a pleasant lie at the shareholder meeting.
Maria: If we restructure the two weakest divisions and renegotiate the debt, we can survive the quarter and rebuild.
Viktor: Then that's the plan. I want a full, honest accounting from every division head by Friday, and no one gets punished for bringing bad news.
Maria: I'll make the calls.
choices: Maria, you're undermining the team. You're dismissed. We'll find someone more loyal.
This is embarrassing. Let's revise the projections so we look on track while we find a fix.
I need to hear this. Give me the worst news first, get a full honest accounting, and never punish anyone for bringing bad news.
You caught this early, so fix it quietly. If the numbers don't work out, I'll distance myself from it.
assets.theoretical_principle: CEO disease and the value of honest feedback channels (Churchill's worst-news department and Gerstner's opening of communication)
assets.psychological_breakdown: Option 2 embodies the growth-minded leader who confronts brutal facts rather than flattery, like Churchill's department that delivered the worst news and Gerstner's memo opening channels of communication up and down IBM. Option 0 is Iacocca's silencing of critics and the fate Enron imposed on Rich Kinder, whose days were numbered precisely because he asked if they were fooling themselves. Option 1 is Enron's self-deception of recording profits before earning revenues, and option 3 hides responsibility while keeping the appearance of control.
key_concepts: People with the fixed mindset do not admit and correct their deficiencies.
Enron forced its employees to look and act extraordinarily talented, pushing them into the fixed mindset.
Rich Kinder was the only person at the top who constantly asked, 'Are we smoking our own dope?'
Kinder's days were numbered, but he bought the valuable pipelines and built a company worth seven billion dollars.
CEO disease is the fixed-mindset peril where leaders surround themselves with good news despite warning signs.
A company that cannot self-correct cannot thrive.
Churchill set up a special department whose job was to give him all the worst news.
Gerstner sent a memo to every IBM worker six days after arriving, promising to meet and talk about strengthening the company.
Growth-minded leaders look squarely at their own mistakes and ask what skills they and the company will need in the future.
The fixed mindset lets CEOs create a world that caters to their need for validation.
assets.theory_summary: This dialogue tests CEO disease, the fixed-mindset leader's tendency to surround himself with validating good news, against the growth-minded practice of demanding honest feedback. Dweck shows self-correcting companies like those led by Gerstner opened channels for bad news, while Enron silenced the one executive who asked if they were fooling themselves.

credibility.basis: Empirical education psychology (Dweck's mindset research; replication nuance)

assets.domain: Growth vs. Fixed Mindset | Attribution Theory
assets.topic: The Fixed-Mindset CEO and the Growth Turnaround
assets.visual_frame_description: A fictionalized boardroom on the evening of a quarterly review: a charismatic autocrat stands before a rising stock chart while his top operations officer asks whether the revenue projections are real. Behind the CEO, a wall of Employee of the Day plaques and framed magazine covers signals a company obsessed with looking brilliant, while a finance director in the corner quietly holds a report labeled Revised Forecast Downward.
assets.player_mission: Diagnose the mindset pattern at work in this boardroom, then choose the signature first move of a new CEO that models what the chapter's growth-minded leaders did to turn companies around.
assets.boss_battle_explanation: The central concept is the fixed-mindset CEO's self-defeating pattern, CEO disease, gargantuan ego, blame and cover-up, and what a growth-minded turnaround requires. Dweck shows that Iacocca, Dunlap, Lay, Skilling, Case, and Levin sacrificed their companies to the need to prove superiority, while Welch, Gerstner, and Mulcahy rooted out the fixed mindset and built cultures of growth and teamwork.
assets.stage_1_observation: The CEO proudly points to a chart of rising stock while his operations officer asks whether the revenue projections are real. The boardroom walls are covered with Employee of the Day plaques and framed magazine covers, and a finance director quietly holds a report labeled Revised Forecast Downward. Everyone in the room except the operations officer seems to be agreeing with the CEO's story.
assets.stage_1_question: Which pattern is operating in this boardroom, and what is its root cause?
assets.stage_1_correct_answer: The company has been forced into a fixed mindset: everyone must look and act extraordinarily talented, so warning signs are suppressed and honest numbers are buried. This is the same dynamic that doomed Enron, which worshiped talent and made a flaw intolerable.
assets.stage_2_intervention: You are the new CEO brought in to save this company. In your first week you must choose a signature move. Which action best models what the chapter's growth-mindset leaders did?
assets.stage_2_correct_answer: Open the channels of communication: send a message to every employee promising honest discussions, disband the elitist inner circle, ask division heads for the worst news first, and protect rather than punish the officer who flagged the fake projections, exactly as Gerstner, Welch, and Churchill did. Attack the elitism and reward teamwork instead of individual genius.
key_concepts: Fixed-mindset leaders live in a world where some people are superior and some are inferior, and the company is a platform to prove superiority.
In more than two-thirds of Jim Collins's comparison leaders, the researchers saw a 'gargantuan personal ego' that hastened the company's demise.
CEO disease is the peril where powerful leaders surround themselves with good news and ignore warning signs.
Iacocca resorted to the fixed mindset's weapons of blame, excuses, and the stifling of critics and rivals.
Albert Dunlap inflated revenues, fired people who questioned him, and covered up Sunbeam's dire straits.
Jeff Skilling believed his genius was profit and recorded millions in profits before a penny of revenue was generated.
Ken Lay wrote of honesty while Enron's ruthlessness thrived, because perception, not reality, was all-important.
Steve Case would rather let the company collapse than let another prince be crowned.
Jack Welch learned there is only a razor's edge between self-confidence and hubris, and that true self-confidence is the courage to be open.
Gerstner disbanded the management committee and attacked elitism, saying 'Hierarchy means very little to me.'
Anne Mulcahy took Balance Sheet 101, told the cold hard truth, cut the employee rolls by 30 percent, yet said 'I'm sorry' and preserved the culture.
Growth-minded leaders use the company as an engine of growth for themselves, the employees, and the company as a whole.
assets.theory_summary: This battle tests the self-defeating arc of the fixed-mindset CEO, ego, blame, cover-up, and the craving for validation, against the growth-minded turnaround practices of Gerstner, Welch, and Mulcahy. Dweck argues the fixed mindset explains where gargantuan egos come from and why they sacrifice their companies.

credibility.basis: Empirical education psychology (Dweck's mindset research; replication nuance)

assets.domain: Growth vs. Fixed Mindset | Attribution Theory
assets.visual_frame_description: A high-rise trading floor at a mid-sized financial firm, where a hallway monitor plays the CEO's speech declaring, 'We hire geniuses here.' On cubicle walls employees quietly track competitors' missteps, and a screen shows anonymized survey answers: 'There is a lot of cheating, taking shortcuts, and cutting corners,' and 'People here hide information and keep secrets.' A team lead whispers to a new hire, 'Never admit a mistake. You'll be labeled.'
assets.player_mission: Diagnose the organizational mindset of this company and the outcomes Dweck's research predicts for its employees, then choose the set of moves that would build a culture of development.
assets.boss_battle_explanation: The central concept is the organizational mindset, the pervasive, company-wide belief that talent is fixed, a culture of genius, or developable, a culture of development, and how leaders weave it into the fabric of the firm. Dweck's study of Fortune 500 and 1000 companies showed this belief predicts trust, commitment, innovation, and ethical behavior.
assets.stage_1_observation: The CEO's speech celebrates hiring geniuses, employees document competitors' missteps, and an internal survey reveals widespread corner-cutting and secret-keeping. A team lead tells a new hire never to admit a mistake, and the company's best performers avoid speaking up. The culture visibly revolves around proving brilliance rather than learning.
assets.stage_1_question: Which organizational mindset does this company embody, and what does the chapter's research predict about its employees?
assets.stage_1_correct_answer: A culture of genius, the fixed mindset: it worships natural talent, and Dweck's data predicts employees will distrust the company, hide information, avoid risk-taking, report more unethical behavior, and express a stronger desire to leave for another firm.
assets.stage_2_intervention: You are the new head of talent, and leadership wants to shift the culture. Which set of moves best creates a culture of development?
assets.stage_2_correct_answer: Present skills as learnable, reward learning and perseverance rather than ready-made genius, give feedback that promotes learning and future success, present managers as resources for coaching, and run a growth-mindset workshop for managers modeled on Heslin's so they notice improvement and coach poor performers instead of labeling them. These are the growth-mindset environment elements the chapter lists.
key_concepts: An organization can have a pervasive belief that talent is just fixed or that talent can be developed in all employees.
Fixed-mindset companies are a 'culture of genius'; growth-mindset companies are a 'culture of development.'
Dweck found strong consensus within each company about whether it held fixed- or growth-mindset beliefs.
Employees in growth-mindset companies have far more trust in the company and a greater sense of empowerment and ownership.
Employees in fixed-mindset companies report more cheating, taking shortcuts, and hiding information.
Employees in growth-mindset companies report that their organization supports reasonable risk-taking and innovation.
Supervisors in growth-mindset companies rate employees as more collaborative, committed to learning, innovative, and higher in management potential.
Fixed-mindset companies search for talent, hire it, and reward it, then ask 'Where's the talent?' because it is not flourishing.
Creating a growth-mindset environment includes presenting skills as learnable and managers as resources for learning.
A growth-mindset workshop can teach managers to detect improvement and coach poor performers.
assets.theory_summary: This battle tests how organizational mindset shapes behavior across a company. Dweck's survey of Fortune 500 and 1000 companies showed a culture of genius breeds distrust, secrecy, and corner-cutting, while a culture of development breeds trust, innovation, and flourishing talent.

credibility.basis: Empirical education psychology (Dweck's mindset research; replication nuance)
